items.title: How We Made a 50-Minute Batch Job Finish Before the Kettle Boils
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Seven fixes, one of them embarrassingly simple, and a robot that compared 3.5 million numbers so we didn’t have to.

Every app has that button. You press it, the spinner starts, and everyone in the room quietly agrees it’s a good time to get coffee.

Ours was called Recompute. It takes about 800 records, recalculates hundreds of derived metrics for each one, ranks every record against all the others, and saves the lot.

  • On the original code, one full run took about 50 minutes.
  • On the first version of our rewrite, it took 7 minutes 54 seconds.
  • After this story, it takes 2 minutes 44 seconds, with the same answers to the sixth decimal place.

This post covers the boring tools, the not-so-boring discoveries, and the one log line that was quietly slowing everything down.

The stack (for context)

  • .NET API, C#
  • Azure Cosmos DB, one JSON document per record (big documents, 100 KB+ of nested data each)
  • SQL Server for the relational bits
  • NLog for logging
  • PowerShell for measuring, Python for checking results
  • Claude Code as a pair programmer for the digging, refactoring and number-crunching

Rule #0: Measure, don’t vibe

Before touching any code, we wrote a tiny PowerShell script that:

  1. sampled the API process’s memory every 5 seconds,
  2. pulled the Recompute log lines with timestamps,
  3. wrote it all to a stats file.
while (-not $done) {
    $p = Get-Process -Id $apiPid
    "{0:HH:mm:ss},{1},{2}" -f (Get-Date), [int]($p.WorkingSet64/1MB), [int]($p.PrivateMemorySize64/1MB) |
        Add-Content $csv
    Start-Sleep 5
}

Every change after that had a before number and an after number. No “feels faster”. We even ran it on a one-core VM to see what happens when you can’t hide behind parallelism. (Answer: 33 minutes. Ouch.)

Fix #1: The JSON parse that happened half a million times

This was the big one.

To rank a record, the code looked at every other record’s metrics. Those were stored as raw JSON, and each time they were needed they got parsed again:

foreach (var other in allRecords)
{
    var metrics = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<MetricsModel>(other.Metrics.Value.ToString());
    // ... rank against it
}

Looks harmless. Now do the maths:

720 records × 720 others = 518,400 JSON parses per ranking pass.

Same JSON, same result, parsed again and again. 🫠

The fix is a cache keyed by the raw JSON object itself, using ConditionalWeakTable:

private static readonly ConditionalWeakTable<JRaw, MetricsModel> Parsed = new();
var metrics = Parsed.GetValue(other.Metrics,
    raw => JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<MetricsModel>(raw.Value.ToString()));

Why ConditionalWeakTable and not a Dictionary?

  • No stale data. When a record is saved again, it gets a new JRaw object, so it's automatically a cache miss.
  • No memory leak. When the old JRaw is garbage collected, its cache entry goes with it.
  • Thread-safe. Fine for parallel workers, since the other records are only read, never changed.

518,400 parses became about 720. That’s the kind of ratio that makes you laugh out loud at your desk.

Fix #2: The log line that wrote itself to a database. Synchronously. Thousands of times.

Here’s a line from the logs, for every single record:

INFO  Calculating step 0
INFO  Calculating step 1
INFO  Calculating step 2
...
INFO  Calculating step 14

Fifteen debug lines per record, left over from someone’s debugging session years ago. That alone is just noise.

But the logger was configured with a database target. Every Info line became a synchronous INSERT into a SQL table. So every save was quietly making dozens of network round trips to write "Calculating step 7" into a log table nobody read.

What we did:

  • Removed the debug lines from the hot path.
  • Took the dump of a big query out of the per-record logs.
  • Kept real errors, of course.
💡 Lesson: check where your logs go, not just what they say. A log line is never “free” if its destination is a database.

Fix #3: One Cosmos client, not one per request

The Cosmos DB SDK docs say it in bold: use a single CosmosClient for the lifetime of the app. Each client owns connection pools, caches account metadata and warms up routing tables.

Our code created clients in a dozen services, per scope. During a Recompute that meant fresh clients, cold caches and repeated handshakes.

The fix was one small helper, so every service gets the same client for the same account:

public static class CosmosClients
{
    private static readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, CosmosClient> Clients = new();
    public static CosmosClient Shared(string endpoint, string key) =>
        Clients.GetOrAdd(endpoint, _ => new CosmosClient(endpoint, key));
}

Thirteen services switched to CosmosClients.Shared(...). Fewer sockets, warm caches, happier database.

Fix #4: Serialize once, send the bytes

To save a record, the code:

  1. serialized the document to JSON to compute a hash (“did anything change?”),
  2. handed the object to the SDK, which serialized it again,
  3. got the whole saved document sent back in the response and deserialized it,
  4. computed the hash a second time a few lines later.

For 100 KB+ documents, that’s real CPU time and real bandwidth.

The new flow:

string json = JsonConvert.SerializeObject(record);   // once
string hash = Hash(json);                             // once, kept in a variable
if (hash == storedHash) return;                       // unchanged? skip the write entirely
using var stream = new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(json));
var response = await container.UpsertItemStreamAsync(stream, new PartitionKey(groupId));
response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

UpsertItemStreamAsync sends your bytes as they are: no second serialization, and no typed object read back from the response.

A nice side effect: on later runs, many records don’t change at all, so the hash check skips their write completely. 🚀

Fix #5: Read reference data once

Some lookup data was read from the database per record, even though it’s the same for the whole run.

We now read it once at the start of the run and pass it down. Not glamorous, but it removed hundreds of round trips.

Fix #6: Stop recomputing what didn’t move

The ranking problem is a fun one. Each record lands in one of five buckets depending on where it sits among all the others. So after you update record #100, records #1 to #99 might have been ranked against stale data.

The original code’s answer was to press Recompute twice: two full passes, about 50 minutes each.

The new flow has three phases:

  1. Own values: compute each record’s own figures. They don’t depend on anyone else.
  2. Shared values: with everyone’s own figures ready, compute the group-wide statistics and rankings and write each record once.
  3. Movers only: check in memory which buckets actually changed, and recompute only those records plus the ones affected by them.

Phase 3 usually touches a handful of records, not 800. One run gives settled, consistent results.

Fix #7 (bonus): A race condition hiding in plain sight

While reading the ranking code we found this:

private static List<Item<T>> firstSlice, secondSlice, thirdSlice, ...;

These are static fields holding per-call working data. With parallel workers, one record's ranking could read another record's slices halfway through. That can produce a bucket that's wrong only sometimes and depends on timing. Those are the worst kind of bugs.

The fix makes them local variables, and the bug is gone. This one wasn’t about speed; it was about getting the right answer at speed.

“But is it correct?” — Comparing 3.5 million numbers

Making things fast is easy if you’re allowed to be wrong. We weren’t.

So we ran the old code on a copy of real data, kept fully separate from the new environment (different database, different document store, different machine), and compared it with the new code’s output.

A Python script:

  • flattened every document into path → value (list items keyed by their name, so reordering didn't count as a change),
  • treated blanks as equal and compared numbers to 1e-6,
  • grouped the differences by field so a human could read them.
Input data       677,542 values   0 differences
Section B        498,268 values   → only the intended "2 decimals instead of 1" change
Section C        831,336 values   → only the intended fix for a junk value
...

Then about 60 rankings moved by exactly one bucket, and we had to know why.

We rebuilt the ranking rule in Python and reran it on both sides’ data:

  • It reproduced 58 of 59 moves exactly.
  • All 58 came from three records whose input data differed between the two copies. Change three values in a ranking of 724 and the bucket boundaries shift by one place.
  • The 59th was the old code storing a bucket that its own rule doesn’t produce.

So the new code was faster and fixed an old ranking error. 🎉

The scoreboard

VersionTime for ~800 recordsOriginal code (needs two runs)~50 min × 2First rewrite7 min 54 sAfter these fixes2 min 44 sFirst rewrite, single CPU core~33 min (parallelism was hiding a lot)

Peak memory stayed around 1.5 GB, and the run finished with zero errors.

What I’d tell past me

  1. Measure first. A 20-line script beat hours of guessing.
  2. Multiply your loops out loud. “Parse the others for each record” sounds fine until you say “half a million parses”.
  3. Find out where your logs go. A log target that’s a database is a hidden I/O cost.
  4. Follow the SDK’s lifetime advice. One client, reused everywhere.
  5. Serialize once. If you already have the bytes, send the bytes.
  6. Do the dependent work last, and only for what changed.
  7. Prove the answers didn’t change. A comparison script is the best confidence you can buy.

And maybe keep the kettle. You won’t need it for this button anymore. ☕

Best,

Komal

items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Thirteen Angular major versions, four defects that compiled perfectly, and the moment we stopped trusting screenshots.

A field report from a thirteen-hop framework upgrade

We finished moving a large internal application from Angular 9 to Angular 22. Thirteen major versions. At the end of it, the thing I keep coming back to isn’t the dependency graph or the migration schematics. It’s this:

Every serious defect we found had already passed a clean build.

Not one of them was a compile error. Several of them survived rounds of screenshot comparison too. The last one survived everything we had, and was caught only because someone typed into a form and watched what happened.

If you are planning a long framework upgrade, the sequencing advice below is useful. But the verification section is the part I’d actually want someone to read.

The ladder you can’t skip

Angular’s updater refuses multi-major jumps, and each version’s migrations exist only as single-step transforms. There is no 9-to-22 path. There are thirteen one-step paths, and you walk all of them.

That sounds tedious and mostly is. The interesting decision isn’t whether to go one at a time — you have no choice — it’s where to cut the phases.

We cut at structural boundaries, not at even intervals. The phases are deliberately uneven: one covers three versions, another covers a single version plus a component-library migration. The rule was that each phase should contain exactly one thing that could plausibly break, so that when something did break, it was attributable.

Two sequencing calls did most of the work.

Move the component library on its own hop

We used a commercial component suite whose versions support ranges of Angular releases. Instead of upgrading it alongside a framework bump, we moved it while sitting still on a framework version it already supported. A problem then belonged to the library alone, with nothing else in flight. One library hop then carried us across three framework versions.

Finish the migration; don’t ship the shim

When Angular Material rebuilt its components on MDC, the official migration deliberately lands you on legacy wrapper components first. Your app looks and behaves identically. It is extremely tempting to stop there.

Two majors later, those wrappers are deleted outright. Had we shipped the shim, that hop would have failed across dozens of files at once, with the component library and the framework both already moved — three variables, one failure, no way to tell which caused it.

So we committed the shim state as its own checkpoint, then did the real migration separately. The later hop reported “no changes required” and passed in an afternoon. That afternoon was bought months earlier.

Libraries break before their peer ranges lapse

Our original risk register assumed a loose peer range meant a library kept working until that range formally excluded you. That assumption is wrong, and it was wrong three separate times.

Three aged dependencies broke during the upgrade. Every one broke earlier than its declared compatibility implied — on internal framework changes, not on a version boundary. All three were roughly four majors behind.

One of them failed especially badly: the visible errors pointed at three unrelated modules of our own code. All three were cascades. The real cause sat further up the output, naming the library. If you ever see a wall of module-level errors after a framework bump, read upward before you start editing your own files.

Four defects that compiled

Here is the part worth your time. Each of these produced a clean build, a clean console, and — for three of them — a screen that looked fine.

1. A hidden file input that wasn’t hidden

We replaced an abandoned file-upload component with a native input and the hidden attribute. Application CSS, written years earlier, overrode it. The control rendered as a stray browser-default button in the middle of a styled form.

Valid HTML. Valid CSS. Passed lint. Visibly broken.

2. Grid headers that truncated the units away

A component-library upgrade restyled grid headers to a single line with an ellipsis. On wide numeric columns, that quietly ate the unit suffix — a header meaning “in millions” became the same header without the millions.

Nothing errored. The number was still right. The meaning of the number was gone, which on a financial grid is worse than a crash, because a crash gets reported.

3. A tab bar that lost its contrast

The MDC migration renamed every internal class. Style overrides written against the old DOM didn’t error — rules targeting a deleted class simply stop applying. The component silently falls back to stock styling.

Our branded tab bar lost its dark background, leaving pale labels on white. That is an accessibility regression, not a restyle, and it shipped a clean build.

4. Form captions that vanished the moment you typed

This is the one that should worry you.

The application captioned its fields with placeholder="…" rather than a label element. The old Material promoted that placeholder into a floating label — the caption sat in the empty field, then floated above it once filled, and stayed visible. MDC does not promote it. The field renders with no label at all and the text behaves like a native placeholder.

So the caption disappeared as soon as a user typed. On a fifteen-field form, a half-completed entry showed fifteen identical underlined boxes and no way to tell which was which.

That fourth one had been live in our own codebase for three phases of verification. Here is why nothing caught it:

CheckWhy it passedbuildValid HTML; placeholder is a legitimate attributescreenshot diffAn empty form renders identically on both versionspayload diffPayloads carry values, not captions — correctly identicalconsoleNothing errored

Every check was blind to it, and each for a different reason. It surfaced only when we filled a field and asked the DOM what caption was still on screen:

before (old framework)
  empty   field text = "Account ID"
  filled  field text = "Account ID"   ← caption survives

after (new framework)
  empty   field text = "Account ID"
  filled  field text = ""         ← no label element at all

The trap where neither library is wrong

My favourite finding, because there is no villain.

Every icon inside a button rendered at under half its previous size. Two entirely reasonable rules collided:

/* the component framework */
.button > .icon { font-size: 1.125rem }
/* the CSS framework, loaded on the same page */
html { font-size: 10px }

Material sizes button icons in rem, assuming the browser default of 16px, where 1.125rem is a sensible 18px. The older CSS framework sets a 10px root — a well-known convention that makes rem arithmetic easy. Against that root, the same rule resolves to 11.25px.

Neither library is at fault. Only the combination fails, and only in an application that carries both. The previous Material had no rem-based rule there, so the conflict simply didn’t exist before the upgrade.

The wider consequence is the useful bit: every rule that framework expresses in rem is being scaled to 62.5% for as long as that root declaration stands. We fixed the icons. The next upgrade will surface more.

And a correction I had to make to myself

My first fix for that didn’t work. I wrote an override matching the framework’s selector specificity exactly, on the reasonable assumption that matching was enough. It isn’t: component styles are injected at runtime, after the static stylesheet, so on a specificity tie the later rule wins.

The build was green. The rule was present in the compiled CSS. The icon was still the wrong size. A build cannot tell you that a CSS rule lost a cascade tie — only measuring the computed value can.

What we actually built to verify

The existing test suite was no help. Of its 135 test blocks, 100 were the CLI’s default “should create” scaffold. A suite like that cannot catch a regression; it can only confirm that components instantiate.

So we built three checks. What makes them worth keeping isn’t that they passed — it’s that each one found something the other two could not see.

Paired visual capture

Twenty screens, old build and new build hit back-to-back against the same backend and the same data, then pixel-diffed.

Two details mattered more than expected. Pair per screen, not per run: an early attempt captured the two builds minutes apart, the database was seeded in between, and we spent an afternoon chasing a difference that was never real. And always capture from production builds — development builds render text sub-pixel-differently, which alone shows up as roughly 2% difference on text-dense screens and drowns the actual signal.

Form payload capture

A visual diff cannot tell you whether a form still submits the same thing. Framework form migrations can change a number into a string, drop a field, or quietly stop firing a validator, all while rendering identically.

So the harness fills every form deterministically, intercepts the outgoing request, captures the body — and aborts the request, so nothing is ever written. Then it diffs the payloads against the pre-upgrade build. Byte-identical, or you have a problem.

DOM measurement

Added last, after the caption bug, and the one I’d add first next time. Ask the rendered document what it actually computed: how tall is this, what font-size resolved, is there a label element, what text remains after typing.

Pixels show you a page. The DOM tells you what the page is.

The through-line

Three of our four defects passed a green build and were caught by looking. The fourth passed looking as well, and was caught only by measuring behaviour.

Comparing pages at rest is not the same as comparing behaviour. A form that looks correct when empty can still be broken in use.

If you take one thing from a thirteen-version upgrade, take that. A compiler proves your code is well-formed. A screenshot proves a page renders. Neither proves the thing works — and on an upgrade, “it still works” is the entire deliverable.

Best,

Komal

We cut at structural boundaries, not at even intervals. The phases are deliberately uneven: one covers three versions, another covers a single version plus a component-library migration. The rule was that each phase should contain exactly one thing that could plausibly break, so that when something did break, it was attributable.

Two sequencing calls did most of the work.

Move the component library on its own hop

We used a commercial component suite whose versions support ranges of Angular releases. Instead of upgrading it alongside a framework bump, we moved it while sitting still on a framework version it already supported. A problem then belonged to the library alone, with nothing else in flight. One library hop then carried us across three framework versions.

Finish the migration; don’t ship the shim

When Angular Material rebuilt its components on MDC, the official migration deliberately lands you on legacy wrapper components first. Your app looks and behaves identically. It is extremely tempting to stop there.

Two majors later, those wrappers are deleted outright. Had we shipped the shim, that hop would have failed across dozens of files at once, with the component library and the framework both already moved — three variables, one failure, no way to tell which caused it.

So we committed the shim state as its own checkpoint, then did the real migration separately. The later hop reported “no changes required” and passed in an afternoon. That afternoon was bought months earlier.

Libraries break before their peer ranges lapse

Our original risk register assumed a loose peer range meant a library kept working until that range formally excluded you. That assumption is wrong, and it was wrong three separate times.

Three aged dependencies broke during the upgrade. Every one broke earlier than its declared compatibility implied — on internal framework changes, not on a version boundary. All three were roughly four majors behind.

One of them failed especially badly: the visible errors pointed at three unrelated modules of our own code. All three were cascades. The real cause sat further up the output, naming the library. If you ever see a wall of module-level errors after a framework bump, read upward before you start editing your own files.

Four defects that compiled

Here is the part worth your time. Each of these produced a clean build, a clean console, and — for three of them — a screen that looked fine.

1. A hidden file input that wasn’t hidden

We replaced an abandoned file-upload component with a native input and the hidden attribute. Application CSS, written years earlier, overrode it. The control rendered as a stray browser-default button in the middle of a styled form.

Valid HTML. Valid CSS. Passed lint. Visibly broken.

2. Grid headers that truncated the units away

A component-library upgrade restyled grid headers to a single line with an ellipsis. On wide numeric columns, that quietly ate the unit suffix — a header meaning “in millions” became the same header without the millions.

Nothing errored. The number was still right. The meaning of the number was gone, which on a financial grid is worse than a crash, because a crash gets reported.

3. A tab bar that lost its contrast

The MDC migration renamed every internal class. Style overrides written against the old DOM didn’t error — rules targeting a deleted class simply stop applying. The component silently falls back to stock styling.

Our branded tab bar lost its dark background, leaving pale labels on white. That is an accessibility regression, not a restyle, and it shipped a clean build.

4. Form captions that vanished the moment you typed

This is the one that should worry you.

The application captioned its fields with placeholder="…" rather than a label element. The old Material promoted that placeholder into a floating label — the caption sat in the empty field, then floated above it once filled, and stayed visible. MDC does not promote it. The field renders with no label at all and the text behaves like a native placeholder.

So the caption disappeared as soon as a user typed. On a fifteen-field form, a half-completed entry showed fifteen identical underlined boxes and no way to tell which was which.

That fourth one had been live in our own codebase for three phases of verification. Here is why nothing caught it:

CheckWhy it passedbuildValid HTML; placeholder is a legitimate attributescreenshot diffAn empty form renders identically on both versionspayload diffPayloads carry values, not captions — correctly identicalconsoleNothing errored

Every check was blind to it, and each for a different reason. It surfaced only when we filled a field and asked the DOM what caption was still on screen:

before (old framework)
  empty   field text = "Account ID"
  filled  field text = "Account ID"   ← caption survives

after (new framework)
  empty   field text = "Account ID"
  filled  field text = ""         ← no label element at all

The trap where neither library is wrong

My favourite finding, because there is no villain.

Every icon inside a button rendered at under half its previous size. Two entirely reasonable rules collided:

/* the component framework */
.button > .icon { font-size: 1.125rem }
/* the CSS framework, loaded on the same page */
html { font-size: 10px }

Material sizes button icons in rem, assuming the browser default of 16px, where 1.125rem is a sensible 18px. The older CSS framework sets a 10px root — a well-known convention that makes rem arithmetic easy. Against that root, the same rule resolves to 11.25px.

Neither library is at fault. Only the combination fails, and only in an application that carries both. The previous Material had no rem-based rule there, so the conflict simply didn’t exist before the upgrade.

The wider consequence is the useful bit: every rule that framework expresses in rem is being scaled to 62.5% for as long as that root declaration stands. We fixed the icons. The next upgrade will surface more.

And a correction I had to make to myself

My first fix for that didn’t work. I wrote an override matching the framework’s selector specificity exactly, on the reasonable assumption that matching was enough. It isn’t: component styles are injected at runtime, after the static stylesheet, so on a specificity tie the later rule wins.

The build was green. The rule was present in the compiled CSS. The icon was still the wrong size. A build cannot tell you that a CSS rule lost a cascade tie — only measuring the computed value can.

What we actually built to verify

The existing test suite was no help. Of its 135 test blocks, 100 were the CLI’s default “should create” scaffold. A suite like that cannot catch a regression; it can only confirm that components instantiate.

So we built three checks. What makes them worth keeping isn’t that they passed — it’s that each one found something the other two could not see.

Paired visual capture

Twenty screens, old build and new build hit back-to-back against the same backend and the same data, then pixel-diffed.

Two details mattered more than expected. Pair per screen, not per run: an early attempt captured the two builds minutes apart, the database was seeded in between, and we spent an afternoon chasing a difference that was never real. And always capture from production builds — development builds render text sub-pixel-differently, which alone shows up as roughly 2% difference on text-dense screens and drowns the actual signal.

Form payload capture

A visual diff cannot tell you whether a form still submits the same thing. Framework form migrations can change a number into a string, drop a field, or quietly stop firing a validator, all while rendering identically.

So the harness fills every form deterministically, intercepts the outgoing request, captures the body — and aborts the request, so nothing is ever written. Then it diffs the payloads against the pre-upgrade build. Byte-identical, or you have a problem.

DOM measurement

Added last, after the caption bug, and the one I’d add first next time. Ask the rendered document what it actually computed: how tall is this, what font-size resolved, is there a label element, what text remains after typing.

Pixels show you a page. The DOM tells you what the page is.

The through-line

Three of our four defects passed a green build and were caught by looking. The fourth passed looking as well, and was caught only by measuring behaviour.

Comparing pages at rest is not the same as comparing behaviour. A form that looks correct when empty can still be broken in use.

If you take one thing from a thirteen-version upgrade, take that. A compiler proves your code is well-formed. A screenshot proves a page renders. Neither proves the thing works — and on an upgrade, “it still works” is the entire deliverable.

Best,

Komal

items.description:
REST, GraphQL, WebSockets, SSE, polling, and friends — because “just fetch the data” is never the whole story.

You click “View Dashboard.”

Somewhere behind the scenes, your frontend sends a request. A server does some work, talks to a database, and sends data back.

Simple, right?

Well… mostly.

Because the moment someone asks, “How does the frontend get data from the server?”, the answer quickly turns into:

“Well, it depends. REST? GraphQL? WebSockets? SSE? Polling? Long polling? gRPC? SOAP? Webhooks? SSR?”

And suddenly, fetching a list of users feels like choosing a communication strategy for an international diplomatic summit.

Let’s break it down.

Not as a boring protocol encyclopedia — but as a practical guide to how data actually travels into your application.

First, the basic relationship

At the simplest level, we have:

Frontend
   │
   │  "Hey, I need some data."
   ▼
Server
   │
   │  Talks to database / services
   ▼
Data
   │
   │  "Here you go."
   ▼
Frontend

The interesting part is how that conversation happens.

Some approaches are request-and-response. Some keep a connection open. Some let the server push updates. Some decide when data should be fetched, while others decide what data should be returned.

Let’s meet the cast.

1. REST API: “Can I get the users, please?”

REST is the familiar, dependable coworker of the API world.

You ask for a resource, and the server responds.

const response = await fetch('/api/users');
const users = await response.json();

Typical REST endpoints might look like:

GET    /api/users
GET    /api/users/123
POST   /api/users
PATCH  /api/users/123
DELETE /api/users/123

The idea is straightforward:

  • GET → Give me something.
  • POST → Here’s something new.
  • PUT → Replace this resource.
  • PATCH → Change part of this resource.
  • DELETE → Remove it.

When REST shines

REST is a great fit for:

  • CRUD applications
  • Admin panels
  • E-commerce APIs
  • Business applications
  • Most standard frontend-backend communication

If you’ve worked with Angular’s HttpClient or React's fetch/Axios ecosystem, you've probably spent a lot of time here.

REST is not the same thing as HTTP. REST is an architectural style; HTTP is the protocol commonly used to carry those requests.

Think of REST as the rules of the conversation, and HTTP as the road the conversation travels on.

2. GraphQL: “I’ll have exactly these fields, thanks.”

REST often gives you a predefined response shape.

GraphQL takes a different approach: the client describes the data it needs.

Imagine a dashboard that needs a user’s name, their recent orders, and the total amount spent.

Instead of calling several endpoints — or receiving a huge response containing things you don’t need — you can ask for a specific shape:

query {
  user(id: "123") {
    name
    email
    orders {
      id
      total
    }
  }
}

The response mirrors the query:

{
  "data": {
    "user": {
      "name": "Komi",
      "email": "komi@example.com",
      "orders": [
        { "id": "1", "total": 2500 }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Why developers like it

  • The client requests only the fields it needs.
  • Related data can be fetched through one query.
  • The schema provides a strongly typed contract.
  • It can reduce the need for multiple round trips for complex screens.

The trade-off

GraphQL isn’t automatically better than REST.

It introduces its own complexity around:

  • Schema design
  • Caching
  • Authorization
  • Query complexity
  • N+1 resolver problems
  • Error handling

Use it when flexible data querying is genuinely valuable — not just because the name sounds fancy.

3. Polling: “Hey… anything new?”

Polling is the frontend equivalent of repeatedly checking your phone.

Frontend: Anything new?
Server: No.

Frontend: Anything new?
Server: No.

Frontend: Anything new?
Server: YES. Here's your data.

In code:

setInterval(async () => {
  const response = await fetch('/api/order-status');
  const status = await response.json();

console.log(status);
}, 5000);

When polling makes sense

  • Order tracking
  • Periodic dashboard refreshes
  • Background job status
  • Data that changes occasionally
  • Systems where real-time infrastructure isn’t necessary

The downside

If nothing changes, you’re still making requests.

That’s like asking your colleague every five seconds whether the deployment is done while they’re still writing the first line.

Simple? Yes. Efficient in every situation? Absolutely not.

4. Long Polling: “Tell me when something happens.”

Long polling improves on ordinary polling.

Instead of responding immediately, the server holds the request open until new data is available — or a timeout occurs.

Frontend → "Any new notifications?"
              │
              │  Server waits...
              │
              ▼
Frontend ← "Yes! Here's one."
              │
              ▼
Frontend → Opens another request

Compared with normal polling:

Normal pollingLong pollingServer responds immediatelyServer waits for new dataClient waits, then asks againClient receives response when data arrivesCan create many unnecessary requestsCan reduce unnecessary empty responses

Long polling was especially useful before persistent real-time connections became commonplace.

It’s not as fashionable today, but legacy systems have a long memory.

5. Server-Sent Events (SSE): “Keep me updated.”

SSE is for one-way, server-to-client streaming.

The browser opens a connection, and the server can keep sending events over it.

const events = new EventSource('/api/notifications');
events.onmessage = (event) => {
  const notification = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log(notification);
};

The server might send events like:

data: {"message":"Build started"}
data: {"message":"Running tests"}
data: {"message":"Build completed"}

SSE is great for

  • Live notifications
  • Activity feeds
  • Deployment logs
  • Streaming AI responses
  • Live status updates

Why not just use WebSockets?

Because sometimes you don’t need a two-way conversation.

If the server is saying:

“Here’s the latest update. Here’s another one. And another one.”

…SSE is a very natural fit.

SSE = server talks, client listens.

6. WebSockets: “Let’s keep the conversation open.”

WebSockets are designed for persistent, bidirectional communication.

Unlike a typical request-response interaction, both sides can send messages whenever needed.

const socket = new WebSocket('wss://example.com/socket');
socket.onopen = () => {
  socket.send(JSON.stringify({
    type: 'join',
    roomId: '123'
  }));
};
socket.onmessage = (event) => {
  const message = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log(message);
};

The connection stays open:

Client  ←────────────────────→  Server
        messages in both directions

Where WebSockets shine

  • Chat applications
  • Multiplayer games
  • Collaborative editing
  • Live trading interfaces
  • Real-time operational dashboards
  • Presence indicators

WebSockets vs SSE

WebSocketsSSECommunicationTwo-wayServer → clientConnectionPersistentPersistentBest forInteractive real-time appsServer-driven updatesBrowser APIWebSocketEventSource

Don’t use WebSockets just because “real-time” sounds impressive. If the client only needs a stream of updates, SSE may be simpler.

7. Streaming HTTP: “Don’t wait for the whole answer.”

Traditional HTTP often feels like:

Request → [wait] → Complete response

Streaming changes the experience:

Request → First chunk → Second chunk → Third chunk → Done

Instead of waiting for the entire response to be generated, the client can process data incrementally.

This is especially useful for:

  • AI-generated responses
  • Large exports
  • Log streams
  • Progressive content
  • Long-running operations

For example, an AI assistant doesn’t necessarily need to wait until the entire answer is written before showing anything. It can display the response as it arrives.

Streaming isn’t necessarily a separate API style like REST. It’s a way of delivering a response progressively, often over HTTP.

8. gRPC: “Let’s call a strongly typed remote method.”

REST is resource-oriented:

GET /users/123

gRPC is more procedure-oriented:

GetUser({ id: "123" })

You define a service contract, commonly using Protocol Buffers:

service UserService {
  rpc GetUser(GetUserRequest) returns (User);
}

Then generated clients can call that method.

Why teams use gRPC

  • Strongly typed contracts
  • Efficient binary serialization with Protocol Buffers
  • Code generation
  • Excellent service-to-service communication
  • Streaming support
  • Good fit for microservices

What about the browser?

Browsers don’t natively use ordinary gRPC the same way backend services do. gRPC-Web provides a browser-compatible approach, commonly with a proxy or compatible server setup.

For a typical Angular business application, REST may be more convenient. For internal microservices, gRPC can be an excellent choice.

9. SOAP: “Please observe the enterprise protocol.”

SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol that has been powering enterprise integrations for years.

A request might look like:

<soap:Envelope>
  <soap:Body>
    <GetUser>
      <UserId>123</UserId>
    </GetUser>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

It’s common in systems involving:

  • Banking
  • Government services
  • Enterprise integrations
  • Legacy platforms
  • Systems requiring formal service contracts

If REST is the developer saying, “Here’s a JSON response,” SOAP is the developer saying, “Please find attached the XML envelope, according to the agreed specification.”

Does SOAP still matter?

Absolutely — especially if you’re integrating with existing enterprise systems.

Modern frontend applications often don’t call SOAP directly. Instead:

Frontend → Your Backend → SOAP Service

The backend acts as an adapter, translating between modern frontend needs and the legacy service.

10. Webhooks: “I won’t keep asking. You tell me.”

Webhooks are slightly different from the others.

They’re generally server-to-server event notifications.

Instead of your system repeatedly asking a payment provider whether a payment succeeded, the payment provider calls your backend when it happens.

Payment Provider
       │
       │ POST /webhooks/payment
       ▼
Your Backend
       │
       ▼
Database updated
       │
       ▼
Frontend gets the latest state

For example:

“Payment successful. Here’s the event.”

Your backend receives it, verifies it, updates the database, and your frontend can then display the updated status.

Common webhook use cases

  • Payment events
  • GitHub events
  • Third-party integrations
  • Order status changes
  • Background processing notifications

Important: A webhook is usually not the frontend fetching data directly. It’s an event delivery mechanism between systems.

Bonus: SSR and Static Generation

Now let’s talk about two approaches that answer a slightly different question:

“When should the data be fetched and where should the page be rendered?”

Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

The server fetches the data, renders the HTML, and sends the result to the browser.

Browser → Server
             │
             ├── Fetch data
             ├── Render HTML
             └── Return HTML

Examples include Angular SSR and Next.js SSR.

This can improve initial page rendering and SEO for suitable applications.

Static Generation

The data is fetched during the build process, and the generated output is served later.

Great for:

  • Blogs
  • Documentation
  • Marketing pages
  • Content that doesn’t change frequently

But remember:

SSR and static generation are rendering strategies, not replacements for REST, GraphQL, or WebSockets.

A server-rendered page can still use REST internally. A statically generated page can still fetch fresh data from an API after loading.

So… which one should you use?

Here’s the practical cheat sheet.

RequirementA good starting pointFetch users, products, ordersRESTRequest flexible, nested dataGraphQLRefresh status every few secondsPollingWait for occasional updatesLong pollingStream server updates one waySSETwo-way real-time interactionWebSocketsStream a response progressivelyStreaming HTTPInternal service-to-service callsgRPCIntegrate with legacy enterprise systemsSOAPReceive events from third-party servicesWebhooksRender HTML on the serverSSRServe build-time content quicklyStatic generation

Of course, real systems mix these.

A modern application might look like:

┌─────────────────────┐
                    │      Frontend       │
                    │   Angular / React   │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                 │             │             │
              REST          WebSocket       SSE
                 │             │             │
                 ▼             ▼             ▼
           ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
           │             Backend                │
           │       API + Business Logic         │
           └───────────────┬────────────────────┘
                           │
                  ┌────────┴────────┐
                  ▼                 ▼
              Database          Other Services

The frontend doesn’t need to know every detail of the infrastructure. It needs to know which communication pattern fits the feature.

The real takeaway

The question isn’t just:

“How do I get data from the server?”

It’s:

“What kind of conversation does my application need to have with the server?”
  • Need something once? Request-response.
  • Need to check periodically? Polling.
  • Need updates as they happen? SSE.
  • Need a two-way live connection? WebSockets.
  • Need only selected fields? GraphQL.
  • Need efficient internal service communication? gRPC.
  • Need another service to notify your backend? Webhooks.
  • Need HTML ready before it reaches the browser? SSR.

And that’s the fun part of frontend engineering: we’re not just rendering data.

We’re choosing how, when, and why that data should arrive.

Best,

Komal

  • Presence indicators

WebSockets vs SSE

Don’t use WebSockets just because “real-time” sounds impressive. If the client only needs a stream of updates, SSE may be simpler.

7. Streaming HTTP: “Don’t wait for the whole answer.”

Traditional HTTP often feels like:

Request → [wait] → Complete response

Streaming changes the experience:

Request → First chunk → Second chunk → Third chunk → Done

Instead of waiting for the entire response to be generated, the client can process data incrementally.

This is especially useful for:

  • AI-generated responses
  • Large exports
  • Log streams
  • Progressive content
  • Long-running operations

For example, an AI assistant doesn’t necessarily need to wait until the entire answer is written before showing anything. It can display the response as it arrives.

Streaming isn’t necessarily a separate API style like REST. It’s a way of delivering a response progressively, often over HTTP.

8. gRPC: “Let’s call a strongly typed remote method.”

REST is resource-oriented:

GET /users/123

gRPC is more procedure-oriented:

GetUser({ id: "123" })

You define a service contract, commonly using Protocol Buffers:

}

Then generated clients can call that method.

  • Strongly typed contracts
  • Efficient binary serialization with Protocol Buffers
  • Code generation
  • Excellent service-to-service communication
  • Streaming support
  • Good fit for microservices

What about the browser?

For a typical Angular business application, REST may be more convenient. For internal microservices, gRPC can be an excellent choice.

9. SOAP: “Please observe the enterprise protocol.”

SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol that has been powering enterprise integrations for years.

  <soap:Body>
    <GetUser>
      <UserId>123</UserId>
    </GetUser>
  </soap:Body>

  • Banking
  • Government services
  • Enterprise integrations

Absolutely — especially if you’re integrating with existing enterprise systems.

Modern frontend applications often don’t call SOAP directly. Instead:

The backend acts as an adapter, translating between modern frontend needs and the legacy service.

Webhooks are slightly different from the others.

       ▼
Your Backend
       │
       ▼
Database updated
       │
       ▼
Frontend gets the latest state

  • Third-party integrations
  • Order status changes
  • Background processing notifications

The server fetches the data, renders the HTML, and sends the result to the browser.

The data is fetched during the build process, and the generated output is served later.

Great for:

  • Blogs
  • Documentation
  • Marketing pages
  • Content that doesn’t change frequently

But remember:

SSR and static generation are rendering strategies, not replacements for REST, GraphQL, or WebSockets.

So… which one should you use?

RequirementA good starting pointFetch users, products, ordersRESTRequest flexible, nested dataGraphQLRefresh status every few secondsPollingWait for occasional updatesLong pollingStream server updates one waySSETwo-way real-time interactionWebSocketsStream a response progressivelyStreaming HTTPInternal service-to-service callsgRPCIntegrate with legacy enterprise systemsSOAPReceive events from third-party servicesWebhooksRender HTML on the serverSSRServe build-time content quicklyStatic generation

Of course, real systems mix these.

A modern application might look like:

┌─────────────────────┐
                    │      Frontend       │
                    │   Angular / React   │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                 │             │             │
              REST          WebSocket       SSE
                 │             │             │
                 ▼             ▼             ▼
           ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
           │             Backend                │
           │       API + Business Logic         │
           └───────────────┬────────────────────┘
                           │
                  ┌────────┴────────┐
                  ▼                 ▼

items.title: Your Team Doesn’t Need More AI. It Needs Less Fear.
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Because the fastest way to slow down an engineering team is to make everyone afraid of being replaced.

There is a funny thing happening in tech right now.

We have AI that can write code, generate tests, explain legacy systems, create documentation, refactor functions, and probably make your morning coffee if you give it the right MCP server.

And yet somehow…

Teams are still stuck.

Projects still miss deadlines.

Engineers still spend hours waiting for approvals.

Product and engineering still misunderstand each other.

Meetings still multiply like rabbits.

And sometimes, the biggest productivity problem isn’t a missing AI tool.

It’s the culture.

The original discussion that inspired this article makes a similar argument: AI can improve productivity, but only when the environment around it is healthy.

And honestly, this deserves a deeper look.

Imagine Giving a Ferrari to a Team That Doesn’t Know Where It’s Going

Let’s say I give your engineering team the most powerful AI coding agent available.

It can write code 10x faster.

Amazing.

Now imagine your team has:

  • unclear requirements
  • five layers of approval
  • no ownership
  • terrible documentation
  • constant priority changes
  • fear of making mistakes
  • managers who blame people when things go wrong
  • teams that don’t trust each other

Congratulations.

You just created a very fast way to build the wrong thing.

AI didn’t solve the productivity problem.

It multiplied it.

That’s the part of the AI productivity conversation that gets conveniently skipped.

Speed isn’t productivity if you’re moving in the wrong direction.

The Real Productivity Stack

We often think productivity looks like this:

AI → Faster Code → Faster Delivery → More Business Value

But real engineering productivity is closer to:

Culture → Clarity → Trust → Good Decisions → Good Architecture → AI → Faster Execution

Notice where AI appears?

Not at the beginning.

Because AI is an accelerator.

And accelerators don’t decide where you’re going.

Your organization does.

Culture Is the Invisible Architecture

We spend enormous amounts of time designing software architecture.

Microservices.

Event-driven systems.

Caching.

Queues.

Load balancers.

Distributed databases.

But there is another architecture that determines how your software behaves:

The architecture of your organization.

Who talks to whom?

Who makes decisions?

Who owns the problem?

Who gets blamed?

Who can challenge a decision?

Who needs permission?

Who has the context?

These things eventually show up in the product.

This connects beautifully with Conway’s Law: organizations tend to produce systems that mirror their communication structures. The article uses this principle to explain why organizational culture and communication have such a direct impact on the products teams build.

If your teams communicate through six layers of management…

Don’t be surprised when your architecture has six layers of unnecessary complexity.

If teams don’t talk to each other…

Don’t be surprised when your services don’t talk to each other properly either.

Your architecture often tells the story of your org chart.

The Most Expensive Bug Is Fear

Here’s something interesting.

A developer who is afraid of being blamed behaves differently from one who feels safe.

The first developer thinks:

“How do I make sure nobody can blame me?”

The second thinks:

“How do I make this better?”

Those are completely different optimization functions.

Fear produces:

  • defensive coding
  • excessive approvals
  • hiding mistakes
  • avoiding difficult decisions
  • less experimentation
  • less communication

Trust produces:

  • ownership
  • faster decisions
  • honest feedback
  • experimentation
  • knowledge sharing
  • better problem solving

You don’t need a new productivity dashboard to measure this.

You’ll see it in the speed at which people say:

“I don’t know, but let’s figure it out.”

versus:

“That’s not my responsibility.”

And Then AI Arrived

AI has made this conversation even more important.

Because AI doesn’t just accelerate good engineering.

It can accelerate bad engineering too.

Bad architecture + AI = more bad code.

Unclear requirements + AI = more code nobody actually needed.

Bad communication + AI = faster misunderstandings.

No review culture + AI = faster technical debt.

Weak engineering practices + AI = technical debt at machine speed.

In other words:

AI doesn’t magically fix organizational problems. It can make them scale.

The original article makes this point particularly well: AI can amplify the conditions that already exist inside an organization.

So before asking:

“Which AI tool should our engineers use?”

Maybe ask:

“What happens when an engineer makes a mistake here?”

That’s a much more interesting question.

Stop Saying “AI Will Replace Engineers”

There is perhaps no faster way to destroy psychological safety than telling your engineers:

“AI can build this now. We don’t need as many people.”

Even if your intention is to motivate AI adoption, the message people hear is:

“Become dramatically more productive or become unnecessary.”

That’s not an AI adoption strategy.

That’s a threat.

And threatened people don’t experiment particularly well.

They protect themselves.

They minimize risk.

They stop volunteering ideas.

They stop challenging decisions.

They stop telling you when something is broken.

Which is exactly when your organization becomes dangerous.

What If We Changed the Message?

Instead of:

“AI means you should produce 5x more.”

Try:

“AI gives you leverage. Let’s figure out how we can use that leverage to solve bigger problems.”

Huge difference.

One creates pressure.

The other creates curiosity.

Great engineers have always adopted better tools.

Compilers replaced manual machine-code work.

IDEs replaced primitive editors.

Cloud platforms changed infrastructure.

Containers changed deployment.

CI/CD changed software delivery.

AI is another major shift in the toolbox.

The goal shouldn’t be:

“How do we force everyone to use AI?”

The goal should be:

“How do we help great engineers use AI to become even more effective?”

That’s a leadership problem, not a tooling problem.

So What Does a Healthy Engineering Culture Actually Look Like?

Forget the fancy culture posters.

Ask these questions:

1. Can engineers make decisions?

Or does every small decision require three approvals and a meeting about the meeting?

2. Can someone challenge the CTO?

Not disrespectfully.

Not politically.

But technically?

If the answer is no, you’re not getting the best ideas from your smartest people.

3. Are mistakes investigated or punished?

If every incident becomes a hunt for “who caused this,” people will eventually learn to hide problems.

4. Does everyone understand the “why”?

Engineers don’t need to know every business detail.

But they should understand what problem they’re solving.

Otherwise, you’re optimizing code instead of outcomes.

5. Do teams trust each other?

If frontend blames backend, backend blames QA, QA blames product, and product blames engineering…

Congratulations.

You have successfully implemented Distributed Blame Architecture™.

Highly scalable.

Terrible availability.

The Best AI Strategy Might Not Be an AI Strategy

This sounds counterintuitive.

But perhaps the first step toward becoming an AI-native engineering organization isn’t buying another AI tool.

It’s fixing the things AI can’t magically fix:

Clear ownership.

Good documentation.

Strong architecture.

Fast decision-making.

Healthy disagreement.

Psychological safety.

Good engineering leadership.

Clear product priorities.

Then bring AI into that environment.

Now you have something powerful.

Because the AI isn’t replacing the organization.

It’s multiplying it.

Don’t Make Your Team 10x Faster at Being Wrong

This might be my favorite way to think about AI productivity.

If your team is already excellent, AI can give them leverage.

If your team is confused, AI can create more confusion.

If your architecture is strong, AI can help you move faster.

If your architecture is a mess, AI can help you create a bigger mess before lunch.

If your culture encourages experimentation, AI becomes incredibly exciting.

If your culture is built around fear, AI becomes another reason people are nervous.

So perhaps the real AI productivity equation isn’t:

AI = More Output

It’s:

AI × Culture × Clarity × Architecture = Actual Productivity

And if any of those multipliers approaches zero…

Well…

Your fancy AI subscription isn’t going to save you.

The Real Competitive Advantage

The companies that win the AI era won’t necessarily be the ones with the most AI tools.

They’ll be the ones where talented people can:

Think → Decide → Build → Learn → Improve

without unnecessary friction.

AI can make each step faster.

But humans still need to decide what deserves to be built in the first place.

That’s why the most important question for an engineering leader isn’t:

“How do I get my engineers to use AI?”

It’s:

“How do I build an environment where great engineers can do their best work — and then give them AI to multiply that ability?”

Because a great culture doesn’t just make people happier.

It makes decisions faster.

Communication better.

Architecture healthier.

Execution smoother.

And yes…

It makes AI dramatically more useful.

Maybe AI isn’t the productivity revolution we should be talking about.

Maybe the real revolution is finally realizing that people were the productivity multiplier all along.

Best,

Komal

items.title: AI Agents Need More Than Context: How LinkedIn Is Building a Memory System for AI
items.author: komal shehzadi
items.description:
Most AI assistants have a short-term memory problem.

You can spend 20 minutes explaining what you want, refining your requirements, correcting the AI, and showing it what you prefer.

Then the conversation ends.

Start a new conversation tomorrow, and the agent often starts from zero.

That might be acceptable for a chatbot.

But it becomes a serious limitation when AI agents are expected to work with us over days, weeks, or months.

Imagine a recruiting assistant that doesn’t just understand the job you’re hiring for today, but gradually learns:

  • which candidates you usually prefer
  • which skills you consider important
  • which locations you avoid
  • how you trade off seniority against experience
  • what kind of candidates you tend to reject
  • and even how you personally approach hiring

This is the problem LinkedIn set out to solve with its Cognitive Memory Agent.

And the interesting part isn’t simply that it “stores memories.”

The interesting part is how it decides what becomes memory in the first place.

The Problem: An AI Agent With No Memory Is Basically Starting Over

Let’s take a simple example.

Suppose you’re a recruiter hiring a Senior Backend Engineer.

You tell an AI agent:

“I’m looking for someone with strong distributed systems experience.”

The agent shows you candidates.

You reject several of them.

Then you say:

“Actually, don’t prioritize candidates from very large companies. I prefer people who’ve worked in smaller engineering teams.”

Later:

“Location isn’t that important. I’m more interested in system design experience.”

Eventually, the agent starts understanding your preferences.

But here’s the problem:

Where does that understanding live?

You could dump the entire conversation into the next prompt.

But conversations grow.

And grow.

And grow.

Eventually, you’re sending enormous amounts of historical context to the model just to answer a relatively simple question.

That’s expensive.

It’s slow.

And worse, most of that information is noise.

The real challenge isn’t:

“How do we store everything?”

It’s:

“How do we remember the right things?”

That’s a much harder engineering problem.

From Chat History to Cognitive Memory

LinkedIn’s approach treats memory as a proper system rather than simply a database of previous conversations.

Their Cognitive Memory Agent was built to provide a persistent state for LinkedIn’s hiring assistant.

Instead of treating every interaction as an isolated session, the system continuously extracts useful information from those interactions and organizes it into different types of memory.

The system has four major layers:

  1. Conversational memory
  2. Episodic memory
  3. Semantic memory
  4. Procedural memory

Think of them as different ways your brain remembers things.

1. Conversational Memory: What Are We Talking About Right Now?

This is the simplest layer.

Imagine you’re currently having a conversation with the recruiting agent.

You say:

“Show me candidates with Python and distributed systems experience.”

Then:

“Actually, prioritize Kubernetes.”

Then:

“Don’t worry about location.”

The agent needs to remember these details while the current task is happening.

That’s conversational memory.

It’s the working memory of the agent.

The problem is that conversational memory doesn’t scale very well.

If the conversation lasts 100 messages, do we really want to send all 100 messages to the model every time?

Probably not.

So the system needs to continuously compress and organize that information.

And that’s where things get interesting.

2. Episodic Memory: What Happened?

Episodic memory stores specific events.

For example:

“On August 20, the recruiter rejected Candidate A because they lacked distributed systems experience.”

Or:

“The recruiter preferred Candidate B because they had Kubernetes experience.”

This is useful because it preserves specific historical evidence.

And there’s another important property here:

Provenance.

Suppose the system eventually concludes:

“This recruiter strongly prefers Kubernetes experience.”

Where did that conclusion come from?

A trustworthy memory system shouldn’t just say:

“The AI thinks this is true.”

It should be able to trace the preference back to actual interactions.

For example:

Preference:
"Kubernetes experience is highly important"

Evidence:
├── Rejected candidate X
│   └── Reason: no Kubernetes experience
├── Preferred candidate Y
│   └── Reason: strong Kubernetes background
└── Explicit instruction
    └── "Prioritize Kubernetes"

This distinction is incredibly important.

The system isn’t simply remembering what it believes.

It’s remembering why it believes it.

3. Semantic Memory: What Have We Learned About You?

Now we move from individual events to generalized knowledge.

Suppose over the last several weeks a recruiter repeatedly:

  • prioritizes distributed systems

One machine wasn’t enough anymore.

🕰️ Before load balancers: one server, one prayer

The early web was beautifully simple:

User
  ↓
Web Server
  ↓
Database

One server. One app. One database. One hopefully-happy sysadmin.

At that point you had two options.

Option 1 — Buy a bigger machine (vertical scaling)

Small Server
     ↓
Bigger Server
     ↓
Even Bigger Server
     ↓
"Why does this server cost more than my house?"

It works. Until it doesn’t. There is always a physical ceiling, the price curve gets ugly long before you reach it, and upgrades usually mean downtime.

And when that one magnificent machine crashes, your entire application crashes with it.

Option 2 — Add more machines (horizontal scaling)

┌── Server 1
User ──┼── Server 2
       └── Server 3

Cheaper boxes, no hard ceiling, and no single machine whose death is fatal.

But now there is a new question: who decides which server gets the request?

Because you really don’t want users doing it themselves:

🚦 Enter the load balancer

A load balancer sits between your clients and your servers.

┌──► Server 1
                  │
Users ──► LB ─────┼──► Server 2
                  │
                  └──► Server 3

The client never learns which server answered. It talks to one address:

api.myapp.com

The load balancer works out the rest. That’s the whole abstraction, and it’s a good one:

One public endpoint. Many interchangeable backends.

1. Performance

Ten thousand requests per second can flatten a single server. Spread across five, it’s a Tuesday.

10,000 req/s
Server 1 → 2,000
Server 2 → 2,000
Server 3 → 2,000
Server 4 → 2,000
Server 5 → 2,000

2. Availability

Server 2 dies. 💥

The load balancer notices it is unhealthy and stops sending it traffic:

┌──► Server 1 ✅
              │
Users ──► LB ─┤    Server 2 ❌
              │
              └──► Server 3 ✅

Users may never notice. That’s high availability — and it’s the part people underestimate. Distributing load is nice; surviving a dead backend is why load balancers are non-negotiable in production.

Tuesday      → 15K
Friday       → 50K

There is no single magical algorithm. There are trade-offs.

Request 1 → Server 1
Request 2 → Server 2
Request 3 → Server 3
Request 4 → Server 1

Server 2 →  8 CPU cores

Server 1 → weight 5
Server 2 → weight 3
Server 3 → weight 2

Server 1 → 100 active
Server 2 →  40 active
Server 3 →  70 active
New request → Server 2

Active connections and capacity. The sensible choice when your fleet isn’t uniform.

Some load balancers factor in observed latency:

Server 2 → 100ms
Server 3 →  35ms

GET /health  →  500        ❌ pull from rotation
GET /health  →  timeout    ❌ pull from rotation

Because the rule is simple:

A dead server should not receive live traffic.

Obvious, isn’t it. And yet production systems find remarkably creative ways to disagree.

Say your app keeps session data in server memory.

User A → Server 1
User B → Server 2
User C → Server 3

  • load stops being balanced — one unlucky server collects all the heavy users
  • autoscaling gets awkward, because fresh instances start out with nobody on them

Redis  ·  Database  ·  Distributed cache

Put shared state there and any server can serve any request. That’s the entire point of stateless application servers — stickiness becomes an optimization instead of a load-bearing dependency.

🌐 Layer 4 vs Layer 7

Layer 4 — transport level

Works with TCP and UDP. It cares about:

IP  ·  Port  ·  Protocol  ·  Connection

It doesn’t read your HTTP request; it shuttles bytes between two sockets.

Fast, cheap, protocol-agnostic. Great for databases, gRPC streams, raw TCP, and anything where you want the payload left alone — including TLS you’d rather terminate on the backend.

Now it speaks HTTP, and can inspect the URL, method, headers, cookies and host:

/api/orders/*  →  Order Service
/images/*      →  Image Server

┌──► User Service
                     │
                     ├──► Order Service
Client ──► LB (L7) ──┤
                     ├──► Payment Service
                     │
                     └──► Notification Service

/api/orders    →  Order Service
/api/payments  →  Payment Service

    ↓
Traffic distribution + health + failover

    ↓

      ↓

Service ──► Sidecar ──► Sidecar ──► Service

Extremely powerful. Also the point at which your architecture diagram starts to look like someone spilled spaghetti on a whiteboard, and your latency budget picks up two extra hops.

That’s a compliment.

Internet
                 ↓
       Cloud Load Balancer
                 ↓
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ↓         ↓         ↓
    Instance  Instance  Instance
       1         2         3

Pair it with autoscaling and capacity follows demand:

Traffic up    →  3 servers → 6 servers
Traffic down  →  6 servers → 3 servers

⚠️ Where it bites

Every component you add is a component you now have to operate. The things that will eventually demand your attention:

The load balancer becomes the single point of failure. If your diagram is:

Users ──► ONE Load Balancer ──► Many Servers

…then you have carefully distributed your servers and invented one new thing that can take the whole site down. 😂 The fix is redundancy at that layer too: an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, anycast, multiple zones — or a managed load balancer, where it’s someone else’s job.

The lost client IP. Behind a proxy, every request appears to come from the load balancer. If you rate-limit or geolocate, you need X-Forwarded-For — and you need to trust only the hops you actually control.

None of this is a reason to skip the load balancer. It’s just the bill.

🧠 The bigger picture

The path most systems walk:

Single Server
     ↓
Vertical Scaling
     ↓
Multiple Servers
     ↓
Load Balancer
     ↓
Auto Scaling
     ↓
Microservices
     ↓
API Gateway / Service Mesh
     ↓
Highly Distributed Systems

The interesting part isn’t the load balancer. It’s the question underneath it:

How do we keep serving users while demand grows and individual components fail?

Distributed systems have been answering that one for decades. The load balancer was just the first honest answer.

🎯 Final takeaway

A load balancer is a traffic manager for your application. It sits between clients and backends and decides where each request goes.

It exists because a single server eventually becomes a bottleneck, and because betting your product on one machine is a genuinely terrifying way to live.

From round robin to Layer 7 routing, health checks, autoscaling, gateways, discovery and meshes — the core idea hasn’t moved:

LOAD BALANCER
                       ↓
             "Who can handle this?"
                       ↓
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ↓            ↓            ↓
       Server 1     Server 2     Server 3
          ✅           ✅           ❌

And that’s the beauty of good infrastructure: when it’s working, nobody knows it’s there.

Your users click a button, and your system quietly decides who should deal with it.

No drama. No melted server. No “please try again later.”

Just traffic going where it should. 🚦

That’s a load balancer.

Best,

Komal

A load balancer is a traffic manager for your application. It sits between clients and backends and decides where each request goes.

                       ↓

          ✅           ✅           ❌

And that’s the beauty of good infrastructure: when it’s working, nobody knows it’s there.

Your users click a button, and your system quietly decides who should deal with it.

Just traffic going where it should. 🚦

That’s a load balancer.
